cards.title: Design emails as image slices, then link buttons in Klaviyo
cards.summary: How to export a Figma email design as slice images, compress them, and rebuild it in Klaviyo with clickable links and alt-ready structure.
cards.use_when: You have approved email creative in Figma and need to ship it through your ESP (Klaviyo) for a campaign or flow.
steps: In Figma, use the Slice tool to cut the email into pieces aligned to where links differ (logo, each CTA, product blocks, footer). Export at 2x for quality, JPEG is fine.

Do not make one giant slice for a long section; oversized image files slow inbox loading. Keep slices roughly small enough that no single image is very large — the source treats ~600px wide sections as the practical outer limit.
Compress all slices before upload (the video used iloveimg.com; any compressor works). Example from the session: 2.84 MB of slices reduced to 469 KB.
In Klaviyo, create a campaign/flow email, delete the default blocks, and add image blocks one by one in order, uploading the compressed slices top to bottom.
Attach links to each image that represents a button so it routes to the correct page (blog, collection, product).
Keep the footer social/footer text area as editable Klaviyo blocks (not images) so you can change social network links and the unsubscribe link.
Add a block of real, visible-but-tiny text in the footer (source suggests size 5) drawn from your About Us copy to counteract an image-heavy email looking spammy to Gmail and help deliverability.
Verify current Klaviyo image-block and campaign interface before executing — UI changes over time.
caveats: Heavy image-only emails risk deliverability; the hidden/tiny text trick is a source recommendation, not a guaranteed deliverability fix.
Email clients may block images; ensure key text is not only inside images where possible.

cards.title: Use a non-discount email strategy: brand, value, social proof
cards.summary: Build a three-email mix of branded, value, and social-proof emails that promote products subtly instead of discounting.
cards.use_when: Planning a campaign calendar or welcome/engagement flow and you want to protect margin rather than default to discount offers.
steps: Decide the angle per email up front: (1) a branded email carrying your brand voice and best sellers, (2) a value/education email, (3) a reviews/social-proof email.
For the branded email, lead with a strong tagline tied to the brand (the session used a 'do gym' angle) and tie it into best sellers.
For the value email, pick a blog post or educational concept that hits a customer pain point (e.g. training at home with dumbbells) and tease the click.
For the social-proof email, pull real testimonials from your site that overcome objections and span different customer types.
Promote products subtly throughout so the email does not feel salesy and add sales resistance, while still giving a clear path to buy.
Find inspiration by scrolling the brand's Instagram and site to mine community language and angles, then carry that into email instead of plain corporate layouts.
caveats: Non-discount emails aim to protect margin but may convert differently than a discount blast; the source presents this as his preferred approach, not a universal rule.

cards.title: Source email angles from your own Instagram and website
cards.summary: Mine brand Instagram captions, community language, and site blogs to generate email ideas instead of designing from a blank page.
cards.use_when: You need campaign angles for a store and want ideas that feel on-brand and content-driven rather than purely promotional.
steps: Scroll the brand's Instagram to capture recurring community language and recurring phrases (the source noticed the brand treated 'gym' as a verb).
Turn a repeated phrase or community theme into a tagline you can build a whole email around.
Check whether the site has a blog and pick a post that addresses a real customer pain point (e.g. home workouts without machines).
For that post, plan a blog email that teases the click and drives traffic back to the site, where readers can also shop.
Pull testimonials from the site for a separate social-proof email.
Note where the brand's email looks corporate/bland versus its livelier Instagram, and set the goal of bringing that life into email.
caveats: This is a content-mining process, not a performance guarantee; the source's claim that it 'prints cash' is his framing.

cards.title: Pick email layouts from an inspiration bank of proven brands
cards.summary: Reuse layouts and sections from successful brands' emails rather than inventing new structures each time.
cards.use_when: You are laying out a new campaign email and need proven section structures for hero, product, and footer blocks.
steps: Keep a swipe inbox/folder of emails from brands you follow so you have a bank of layouts and sections.
Mimic the winning structure for most emails: headline + body copy + button in the hero, especially a 'learn more' button for blog emails.
Prefer centering the hero button and putting it prominently rather than leaving it small and off to the side.
Lift section ideas such as a 'mix and match' product block or a 'chest/back anatomy' educational breakdown and adapt the content to your products.
Keep the CTA goal singular: the source notes you can have many buttons as long as they all push one decision, not several competing ones.
caveats: Copy the structure and layout, not another brand's copyrighted assets or copy.
Button size/placement preferences are the source's tested opinions; test on your own list.

cards.title: Educate with a product 'bridge' section to justify the price
cards.summary: Add an educational section that names product features and ties them to customer benefits to give a reason to buy.
cards.use_when: Designing product or launch emails where the hero alone just says 'shop our shoes' without explaining why the product is good.
steps: After the hero, add a bridge/education section that names concrete product features (the source's example: engineered mesh, dura outsole, 4mm lugs).
Tie each feature to a benefit framed around the customer, not the product in isolation.
For a content/blog email, use the bridge to summarize and add value (e.g. break down the parts of a muscle and their function) so the email teaches something.
Keep teasing the click throughout so the reader goes to the site and can shop.
Use visuals that support the education (labeled images, arrows pointing to parts) to make it feel immersive rather than blocky.
caveats: Feature-to-benefit claims must be accurate for your product; do not invent specs.
The source's specific product specs are examples from one brand, not benchmarks.

cards.title: Build product interest with a GIF 'mix and match' section
cards.summary: Create a flipping GIF that pairs tops and bottoms to help customers visualize a full outfit and click through.
cards.use_when: Designing a merch/bestseller email where you want to show multiple product combinations without a wall of static images.
steps: In Figma, create a 600px-wide frame and place the first product pairing image plus a circle/arrows overlay hinting at flipping.
Duplicate the frame and swap in the next top/bottom combination; repeat so it cycles tops while holding bottoms, then cycles bottoms.
Select all frames and run a GIF plugin (the source uses one called Gif Canvas) to generate the animated file.
Insert the GIF into the email design and verify playback in the preview; static Figma won't animate but the exported GIF will.
Add a 'shop now' button beneath the GIF.
Centering the GIF and giving it a clean button keeps the section usable across clients.
caveats: GIF file size matters for load time — keep the animation reasonably compact.
Verify plugin availability/behavior since Figma plugins can change.

cards.title: Add texture, gradients, and depth so emails don't look flat
cards.summary: Use background texture, gradients, and layering tricks to make branded emails feel immersive rather than blocky.
cards.use_when: Your email sections look like flat white blocks and you want to add life and flow without changing the copy.
steps: Pull a subtle background texture from the brand site and place it behind the hero content, then send it to the back so it doesn't block content.
Use brand logos/logomarks as faint layered elements to add depth without distracting.
To blend a gray section into a white footer, create a full-width rectangle, apply a linear gradient, set the top stop to the section color and the bottom stop to white so it flows.
Use a background-removal plugin to cut a subject out of a photo, then place large outlined type behind the subject for a layered hero effect.
Apply drop shadows to make photographic elements stand out (the source nudges the shadow offset sideways for depth).
Use white/outlined text over dark image areas and add a black-to-transparent gradient behind text to keep it readable.
caveats: Layering and gradients add file size; compress assets before upload.
Verify current plugin names/behavior before relying on them.

cards.title: Reduce thumb stretch: size and place CTAs for mobile taps
cards.summary: Put large, centered CTAs where a phone-holding thumb can easily reach, because small corner buttons hurt clicks.
cards.use_when: Placing buttons in an email hero or product section and deciding size and position for mobile readers.
steps: Avoid small buttons in the top-left corner: the source notes a right-handed thumb has to stretch to reach it, and says this measurably hurts conversions.
Make the primary CTA large enough to be unmissable (the source jokes even a blind person would see it).
Center the hero button and place it prominently rather than burying it.
Underline text links or use a clear 'shop now' button — the source says he has A/B tested this consistently and clicks rise when links are underlined or buttons are explicit.
Vary button placement occasionally so readers don't get the same layout every email, while keeping the key CTA prominent.
Give each product block its own shop-now button, then a general CTA for shoppers who don't want the featured items.
caveats: The thumb-reach and underline claims are the source's tested opinions; validate for your audience.
Button sizing should be checked against your template/rendering across major clients.

cards.title: Give a fallback general CTA plus shop-by-collection at the bottom
cards.summary: Add a broad CTA and category links so shoppers who don't want the featured products still have a path to buy.
cards.use_when: An email features specific products or a niche angle (e.g. yoga) and you want it to convert non-targeted subscribers too.
steps: After listing featured products with their own CTAs, add a general 'shop now' so people who don't like those exact items can still browse.
At the bottom, add shop-by-collection/category links (the source's example used running, workout, casual, yoga) so subscribers not doing that activity still have options.
For activity-specific emails, add a line broadening the relevance (e.g. 'style doesn't stop at the mat') and show products plus testimonials.
End with a large category CTA.
Keep the email working for the whole list, not just the segment the angle targets.
caveats: More CTAs risk diluting the message; the source argues it's fine as long as they point to one overall decision (shopping).

cards.title: Use big aggregate review counts as a trust signal in emails
cards.summary: Surface verified review volume and select testimonials that answer objections to build trust and goodwill.
cards.use_when: Building a social-proof or reviews email, or adding a trust section to a product email.
steps: Use the aggregate verified-review figure (the source's example displayed '100,000+ verified reviews') as a big selling point instead of a precise small number.
Hand-pick testimonials that overcome specific objections and span customer types (the source made sure to include male and female reviewers).
Bold the main points inside each testimonial so the value reads at a glance.
Present testimonials visually (the source put them in framed text boxes on a phone graphic, with star icons made from shape tools).
Frame the email personally with a headline like 'by gym lovers for gym lovers' to counter a corporate feel.
Add a lifestyle photo gallery plus shop-now at the bottom to add life without overwhelming the reader.
Keep it simple: the source skipped featuring products in the social-proof email, focusing on trust, then a shop button.
caveats: The source states testimonials 'always help' based on testing for large brands; that's his opinion, not a universal result.
Display only review numbers you can substantiate.

cards.title: Write blog emails that sell the click and teach on the way
cards.summary: Structure a content email so the reader clicks through to the full post while getting value in the email itself.
cards.use_when: Sending a blog/content email to drive site traffic and downstream purchases.
steps: Lead with headline + body copy + a 'learn more' button at the top so the click is easy.
Tease the content and sell the click in the body (the source framed it as a short list, e.g. 'top 5 dumbbell back exercises').
Add a bridge section that gives real value inline — summarize and break down the topic (the source used a 'back anatomy 101' breakdown of muscle parts and functions) so the email isn't just a teaser.
Connect each educational element back to the blog and site so readers who go deeper can shop.
Include multiple 'learn more' reminders down the email and end with product photos plus the CTA.
Use benefit/motivational copy to sell the click (the source emphasized the exercises work with minimal equipment and space, for busy-gym-to-small-living-room use).
caveats: Multiple CTAs are fine here because they all point to one action (reading the post); don't mix in competing goals.
Keep the inline education accurate and consistent with the linked post.

cards.title: Lay out copy section-by-section before designing
cards.summary: Plan the email's sections and write the copy in a doc first so design and layout follow a clear structure.
cards.use_when: Starting a new campaign email and you want copy organized before touching the design tool.
steps: Lay out the email in a doc as distinct sections (headline, body, button, bridge, product block, footer) so you can see the structure.
Write each section's copy against that plan, matching the winning hero pattern (headline + body + button).

For brand-voice body copy, prompt an AI with the brand's voice and the desired tone (the source asked for two sentences in the brand's voice about the gym) and treat the output as a draft to work with, not final.
Reference successful brands' emails while writing to borrow proven section structures rather than reinventing layout.
Hand the sectioned doc to a designer with clear labels (e.g. 'insert photo gallery of lifestyle pictures', 'mix and match tops and bottoms') so they know what each block needs.
Keep a consistent footer across emails with shop-by buttons (e.g. men/women) and social links.
caveats: AI copy needs brand-voice checking; the source notes you sometimes have to work with the output.
This is a production workflow, not a performance claim.

cards.title: Choose a design tool that supports advanced layout
cards.summary: Prefer a more capable design tool (Figma) over basic tools when building immersive, layered email designs.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to design campaign emails and needing layered type, gradients, background removal, and GIF plugins.
steps: Use Figma for composite/advanced email design: it organizes layers well and supports the plugins needed (background remover, GIF canvas).
Note that the source rates Canva as good but more basic and harder to organize — fine for simpler emails, limited for advanced effects.
Start each email with a 600px-wide frame as the canvas.
Build buttons from a rectangle (set corner radius, e.g. 30) plus a text layer, then color and size them.
Use shapes, images, text, strokes (outline type), gradients, and effects (drop shadow) to build immersive sections.
Verify current plugin availability and UI, since Figma plugins and menus change.
caveats: Tool preference is the source's opinion; use whatever your team can execute well.
Plugin-dependent steps may break if a plugin is removed or renamed.

cards.title: Keep the CTA goal singular even with many buttons
cards.summary: A long email can have many buttons as long as they all drive one decision, not several competing ones.
cards.use_when: Designing a multi-section email and deciding how many CTAs to include.
steps: Pick the single action the email should drive (read the post, shop the collection, shop the product).
Repeat that same CTA down the email (the source used multiple 'learn more' buttons) rather than introducing new, different asks.
Place CTAs after key sections: hero, education bridge, product blocks, and bottom category links.
Avoid telling the customer too many different things in one email; competing goals dilute the click.
Use shop-by buttons in the footer (e.g. men/women) that still funnel toward shopping.
caveats: This is the source's working rule of thumb, not a tested universal law; monitor your own click-through by placement.

cards.title: Compress email images to protect load time
cards.summary: Compress exported email slice images before upload so the email loads fast in the inbox.
cards.use_when: Preparing Figma slice exports for upload to your ESP.
steps: Export slices from Figma (the source exports at 2x for quality, JPEG format).
Run all slices through an image compressor before uploading (the source used iloveimg.com).
Check the size savings: the session went from 2.84 MB to 469 KB with little quality loss.
Keep each slice reasonably small; avoid one giant image for a long section.
Upload compressed slices into your ESP and rebuild the email there.
caveats: Aggressive compression can degrade quality; balance size against visual fidelity.
Verify current compressor interfaces as tools change.

cards.title: Match email design and copy to the brand's voice
cards.summary: Carry the brand's visual identity, fonts, and tone into email so it doesn't read as generic or corporate.
cards.use_when: An email looks bland/corporate compared to the brand's social presence and you want it to feel on-brand.
steps: Use the actual brand font rather than a default font — the source notes it dramatically brings the design to life.
Pull real brand assets: logo, colors, background textures, lifestyle images from the brand's own channels.
Write copy in the brand's voice (the source prompted an AI to write in the brand's voice and then refined it).
Aim for an immersive, fun feel rather than blocky, plain-white sections.
Mirror the energy and community language of the brand's Instagram in the email.
Add life to flat sections with lifestyle imagery and color rather than plain studio product shots.
caveats: Brand-voice copy from AI must be checked against the brand's actual voice.
Visual taste judgments are subjective; the source's '10/10' ratings are his opinion.
